verdict_text:
Done — the tool passed its acceptance check.

What was checked, honestly: The gate runs scheduler.py against two specific input files — a 6-team even case and a 5-team odd case — and checks week count, total real-game count, complete pair coverage with no duplicates, no team playing twice in a single week, sequentially numbered week labels, and even BYE distribution for the odd case. It does not test a 2-team minimum, large leagues, team names containing special characters or the word BYE itself, missing or malformed input files, or output sorting beyond week-label order. A schedule that passes both gate runs is structurally correct for those two sizes; other team counts and input edge cases are outside the gate's scope.

Points that still need a human expert's judgment: Whether home/away designation is required for each game — the circle method can produce balanced home/away splits but the problem statement does not specify this; a league organizer should decide before the scheduler is built. Whether a double round-robin (each pair plays twice, once at each venue) is the intended format rather than a single round-robin — this doubles the number of weeks and should be confirmed with the league.

Check output (last lines): PASS: 6 teams | 5 weeks | 15 games | all criteria satisfied

intent.ask: I help run a small rec soccer league and every season I waste a weekend turning the team list into a week-by-week schedule where every team plays every other team once and nobody plays twice in the same week - can you make me something that does that
intent.inferred_intent: You want a tool that takes your list of teams for the season and automatically builds a round-robin schedule — every team plays every other team exactly once, with no team playing more than one game per week. This would replace the weekend you currently spend doing it by hand each season.
intent.objective: Build a round-robin scheduler that takes a list of rec soccer teams and outputs a week-by-week schedule where every team plays every other team once and no team plays twice in the same week.
questions: How do you want to give it the team list — paste them in when you run it, or put them in a simple text file ahead of time?
What do you want the schedule to look like when it's done — printed to the screen, saved as a file you can share (like a spreadsheet or PDF), or something else?
intent.form_factor_plain: You'll get a small program you run on your computer — type a command, give it your team names, and it prints out (or saves) the full season schedule instantly.

grounding.objective: Build a round-robin scheduler that takes a list of rec soccer teams and outputs a week-by-week schedule where every team plays every other team once and no team plays twice in the same week.
grounding.summary: Recreational soccer league round-robin scheduling is solved in practice with the circle (rotation) algorithm: one team is fixed as an anchor while the remaining teams rotate clockwise each round, producing exactly one matchup between every pair of teams across the full schedule. For N teams the schedule requires N-1 rounds if N is even, or N rounds with one BYE per round if N is odd, and the total number of games equals N*(N-1)/2. A correct output is week-labeled, lists every game pairing once per week, and guarantees each team appears in exactly one game per week. Practitioners treat the circle method as the de-facto standard and flag odd-team handling (BYE distribution) and tiebreaker policy as the two variables requiring explicit decisions before the schedule is usable.

norms.norm: Use the circle (rotation) algorithm: fix one team as an anchor, arrange the remaining teams in a ring, and rotate them clockwise one position after each round to generate all pairings.
norms.source_title: Sports Scheduling Simplified: The Power of the Rotation Algorithm in Round Robin Tournament

norms.norm: For an even number of teams N, produce exactly N-1 rounds; for an odd number, produce N rounds and add a dummy BYE slot so every round still has N/2 pairings (rounded down) with one team sitting out.
norms.source_title: Round Robin Tournament Generator: Format, Formula & Schedule

norms.norm: Verify correctness with the formula: total games must equal N*(N-1)/2, confirming every pair meets exactly once.
norms.source_title: Round Robin Tournament Generator: Format, Formula & Schedule

norms.norm: Each team must appear in at most one game per round (week); a schedule where any team is listed in two games in the same round is considered malformed.
norms.source_title: Sports Scheduling Simplified: The Power of the Rotation Algorithm in Round Robin Tournament

norms.norm: When odd-team BYEs are used, distribute them so each team receives the BYE exactly once across the schedule — unequal BYE distribution is a recognized fairness defect.
norms.source_title: Round Robin Tournament Generator: Format, Formula & Schedule

norms.norm: Output rounds in sequential, labeled order (Week 1, Week 2, …) with each game pairing explicitly listed per round so league administrators can publish and verify the schedule at a glance.
norms.source_title: Sports Scheduling Simplified: The Power of the Rotation Algorithm in Round Robin Tournament

Whether a double round-robin (each pair plays twice, once at each venue) is the intended format rather than a single round-robin — this doubles the number of weeks and should be confirmed with the league.

design.objective: Build a round-robin scheduler that takes a list of rec soccer teams and outputs a week-by-week schedule where every team plays every other team once and no team plays twice in the same week.
design.tool_plan: A command-line Python script called scheduler.py reads a plain text file of team names, one per line, and prints a complete round-robin schedule to stdout. It uses the circle rotation algorithm to pair every team against every other team exactly once, and inserts a BYE dummy entry to distribute rest weeks evenly when the team count is odd. Output is organized by labeled week sections so a league administrator can copy and post the schedule immediately after running the script. A league organizer runs it once at the start of each season, pointing it at their teams file and redirecting the output to a file or spreadsheet as needed.
design.data_shape: Input: a plain text file with one team name per line, no headers, passed as the first command-line argument to scheduler.py. Output: printed to stdout as sequential week sections — each opens with a line reading 'Week N:' followed by one game per line in the format 'Team A vs Team B'; when the team count is odd, the sitting-out team appears as 'Team X vs BYE'. The tool writes no output files itself; the caller redirects stdout if a saved copy is needed. The tool file is scheduler.py, located in the work directory, invoked as: python3 scheduler.py <teams-file>.
design.gate_plain: Done when: given a file of team names the tool prints a schedule where every team plays every other team exactly once, no team is listed in more than one game in any single week, rounds are clearly labeled Week 1 through Week N in ascending order, and if there is an odd number of teams each team sits out exactly once across the full schedule.

gate_criteria.criterion: The total number of real (non-BYE) games across all weeks equals N*(N-1)/2, confirming every pair of teams is scheduled exactly once.
No team name appears in more than one game within the same week section.
For an even number of teams N the output contains exactly N-1 week sections; for an odd number it contains exactly N week sections.
Rounds are labeled sequentially Week 1, Week 2, and so on with each game listed on its own line inside that week's section, and week numbers run consecutively from 1.
When the team count is odd, every team has exactly one BYE across the full schedule — no team sits out twice or never sits out.
Every possible pair of real (non-BYE) teams appears in exactly one game across the full schedule — no matchup is repeated and none is missing.

design.judge_scope: The gate runs scheduler.py against two specific input files — a 6-team even case and a 5-team odd case — and checks week count, total real-game count, complete pair coverage with no duplicates, no team playing twice in a single week, sequentially numbered week labels, and even BYE distribution for the odd case. It does not test a 2-team minimum, large leagues, team names containing special characters or the word BYE itself, missing or malformed input files, or output sorting beyond week-label order. A schedule that passes both gate runs is structurally correct for those two sizes; other team counts and input edge cases are outside the gate's scope.
